A trident is a long spear with three sharp points at one end, instead of just one. Picture a regular spear — now imagine three pointed tips sitting side by side at the top, like three teeth of a fork. That is a trident. The three prongs are usually the same length, equally sharp, and all point in the same direction. The handle is long, like a staff, allowing it to be gripped firmly or even thrown. It is, at once, a weapon, a tool, and one of the most instantly recognized shapes in human history.
The most famous trident — Poseidon and Neptune

The trident is most powerfully linked to Poseidon, the ancient Greek god of the sea, and his Roman counterpart, Neptune. In myths, the trident was Poseidon's personal weapon and the symbol of his authority. He used it to stir up storms, split the earth open, and command the ocean. Just as a king holds a scepter to show he is in charge, Poseidon held a trident. If you have ever seen a statue or painting of Neptune, he is almost always shown as a muscular, bearded figure gripping a long trident. This is exactly why, even today, the trident feels deeply connected to the ocean, to raw natural power, and to the idea of a god or ruler being in control.

Beyond mythology, the trident has had very practical uses across different eras and cultures.

As a fishing tool, the trident was extremely effective. Fishermen would wade into shallow water and spear fish directly. The three prongs were a clever design — even if the fish shifted slightly at the last moment, one of the prongs would still catch it. A single-pointed spear would miss far more often. This use is ancient and was common in many parts of the world.

As a weapon in gladiator combat, the trident played a famous role in ancient Rome. A type of gladiator called the retiarius fought with a trident in one hand and a weighted net in the other. The strategy was to throw the net over the opponent to trap them, then strike with the trident. This style of fighting was well-known and widely watched in Roman arenas.

Over thousands of years, the trident grew beyond being just a physical object and became a loaded symbol recognized across the world.

Because of its association with Poseidon and Neptune, a trident commonly represents mastery over the sea or the forces of nature. It carries a sense of immense, almost unstoppable power.

In Hinduism, the trident is called the trishula and is the weapon and symbol of Shiva, one of the most important gods in the religion. Here it carries deep spiritual meaning — the three prongs represent three fundamental forces: creation, preservation, and destruction. It is widely used in Hindu art, temples, and rituals.

The island nation of Barbados features a trident on its national flag, symbolizing the sea and a break from its colonial past.

Today, the word "trident" is used for many things beyond ancient spears and sea gods. It is the name of nuclear-armed submarines used by the American and British navies — chosen because the word suggests devastating power. It is a popular brand of chewing gum. Sports teams and companies use it in their logos and names. In every case, the word is deliberately chosen to evoke strength, sharpness, and authority.

"The statue of Neptune towered over the fountain, his trident raised toward the sky." "The fisherman stood knee-deep in the river, gripping his trident and watching the water for movement." "On the nation's flag, a golden trident stood against a deep blue background." "In the myth, the god drove his trident into the ground and the earth shook."

A trident is a three-pronged spear — a real historical weapon and fishing tool — that became one of the world's most enduring symbols of power, most famously belonging to the sea god Poseidon, and still widely recognized and used as a symbol today.
